    <div class="guide-header">
        <h1><i class="fas fa-certificate"></i> SOC 2 Compliance Checklist <span class="new-badge"><i

        <p style="color: var(--text-muted); font-size: 1.1rem;">Complete guide to achieving SOC 2 Type II

        <div class="guide-meta">
            <span><i class="fas fa-book-open"></i> 20 min read</span>
            <span><i class="fas fa-crosshairs"></i> Intermediate</span>
            <span><i class="far fa-calendar-alt"></i> December 2025</span>
        </div>
    </div>

    <img src="/images/guides/soc2-compliance-checklist.png" alt="SOC 2 Compliance Checklist" class="featured-image" loading="lazy">

    <div class="info-box">
        <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Why SOC 2:</strong> SOC 2 is the most requested compliance
        framework for SaaS companies. Enterprise customers require it for vendor onboarding. A SOC 2 Type II report
        demonstrates your commitment to security over time.
    </div>

    <div class="toc">
        <h3><i class="fas fa-list-ul"></i> Table of Contents</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><a href="#overview">1. What is SOC 2?</a></li>

        </ul>
    </div>

    <div class="content">
        <h2 id="overview"><i class="fas fa-award"></i> 1. What is SOC 2?</h2>

        <h3>Understanding the Basics</h3>
        <p>Imagine you're a growing SaaS company. You've built an amazing product and you're ready to land your
            first enterprise customer. They're excited too - until their security team asks: <em>"Do you have a SOC
                2 report?"</em></p>

        <p>You don't. The deal stalls. Or worse, dies. This happens to startups <strong>every single day</strong>.
        </p>

        <div class="info-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-lightbulb"></i> Think of it like this:</strong> SOC 2 is like a restaurant's
            health inspection certificate. You COULD eat at a restaurant without seeing their health grade, but most
            people want proof that the kitchen is clean before they trust them with their food. Enterprise customers
            want the same assurance before trusting you with their data.
        </div>

        <h3>Why Enterprise Customers Demand SOC 2</h3>
        <p>Enterprise security teams are responsible for managing vendor risk. When they evaluate your product, they
            need answers to questions like:</p>
        <ul>
            <li>How do you protect our data from hackers?</li>
            <li>What happens if your systems go down?</li>
            <li>Who can access our data in your company?</li>
            <li>How do you handle security incidents?</li>
        </ul>
        <p>Without SOC 2, they'd have to audit you themselves - which takes weeks and costs them money. A SOC 2
            report gives them independent verification that you've already answered these questions properly.</p>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Real Talk for Startups:</strong> If you're selling
            to enterprise (especially Fortune 500 or healthcare/finance), expect SOC 2 to come up in 80%+ of
            security questionnaires. Many enterprises won't even start a pilot without it. Budget 6-12 months and
            $50K-$150K (including prep and audit) for your first SOC 2 Type II.
        </div>

        <h3>The Technical Definition</h3>
        <p><strong>SOC 2</strong> (System and Organization Controls 2) is an auditing standard developed by the
            AICPA (American Institute of Certified Public Accountants) for service organizations. It verifies that a
            company has implemented controls to protect customer data.</p>

        <h3>Who Needs SOC 2?</h3>
        <ul>
            <li><strong>SaaS companies</strong> storing or processing customer data (the most common case)</li>
            <li><strong>Cloud service providers</strong> hosting customer workloads</li>
            <li><strong>Data centers</strong> and managed service providers</li>
            <li><strong>Any B2B company</strong> handling sensitive customer information</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Benefits of SOC 2</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Benefit</th>
                    <th>What It Means</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Win Enterprise Deals</strong></td>
                    <td>Required by most large customers; without it, deals stall or die</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Competitive Advantage</strong></td>
                    <td>Differentiate from competitors who don't have SOC 2</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Risk Reduction</strong></td>
                    <td>The process itself finds and fixes security gaps</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Faster Sales Cycles</strong></td>
                    <td>Security questionnaires get answered in minutes, not weeks</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Operational Improvement</strong></td>
                    <td>Forces you to formalize security processes you should have anyway</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Pro Tip:</strong> If you're pre-revenue or early stage,
            consider using compliance automation tools like Vanta, Drata, or Secureframe. They can cut your SOC 2
            timeline from 12+ months to 3-6 months and reduce costs significantly.
        </div>

        <h2 id="types"><i class="fas fa-clone"></i> 2. SOC 2 Type I vs Type II</h2>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Aspect</th>
                    <th>Type I</th>
                    <th>Type II</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>What It Tests</strong></td>
                    <td>Design of controls at a point in time</td>
                    <td>Design AND operating effectiveness over time</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Time Period</strong></td>
                    <td>Single date (snapshot)</td>
                    <td>Typically 6-12 months</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Rigor</strong></td>
                    <td>Less rigorous</td>
                    <td>More rigorous and valued</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Use Case</strong></td>
                    <td>First-time certification, quick timeline</td>
                    <td>Ongoing compliance, enterprise sales</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Cost</strong></td>
                    <td>$15,000 - $30,000</td>
                    <td>$30,000 - $100,000+</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <div class="warning-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-exclamation-triangle"></i> Important:</strong> Most enterprise customers
            require SOC 2 Type II. Type I is often a stepping stone but won't satisfy security questionnaires
            long-term.
        </div>

        <h2 id="tsc"><i class="fas fa-balance-scale"></i> 3. Trust Services Criteria (TSC)</h2>
        <p>SOC 2 is based on five Trust Services Criteria. Security is required; others are optional based on your
            services:</p>

        <div class="tsc-box">
            <h4><span class="tsc-icon" style="background: #3B82F6;"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i></span>
                Security (Required)</h4>
            <p>Protection of information and systems from unauthorized access. This is the foundation—all SOC 2
                reports include Security.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="tsc-box">
            <h4><span class="tsc-icon" style="background: #10b981;"><i class="fas fa-clock"></i></span> Availability
                (Optional)</h4>
            <p>Systems are available for operation and use as committed. Choose if you have SLAs for uptime.</p>
        </div>

        <div class="tsc-box">
            <h4><span class="tsc-icon" style="background: #f59e0b;"><i class="fas fa-cogs"></i></span> Processing
                Integrity (Optional)</h4>
            <p>System processing is complete, valid, accurate, timely. Choose if data processing accuracy matters.
            </p>
        </div>

        <div class="tsc-box">
            <h4><span class="tsc-icon" style="background: #3B82F6;"><i class="fas fa-lock"></i></span>
                Confidentiality (Optional)</h4>
            <p>Information designated as confidential is protected. Choose if you handle confidential business data.
            </p>
        </div>

        <div class="tsc-box">
            <h4><span class="tsc-icon" style="background: #FF3D3D;"><i class="fas fa-user-shield"></i></span>
                Privacy (Optional)</h4>
            <p>Personal information is collected, used, retained, and disclosed in conformity with commitments.
                Choose if you handle PII.</p>
        </div>

        <h2 id="security"><i class="fas fa-shield-alt"></i> 4. Security (Common Criteria)</h2>
        <p>The Security TSC contains 9 "Common Criteria" (CC) categories:</p>

        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Category</th>
                    <th>Focus</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC1: Control Environment</strong></td>
                    <td>Governance, ethics, oversight structure</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC2: Communication & Information</strong></td>
                    <td>Internal/external communication of policies</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC3: Risk Assessment</strong></td>
                    <td>Risk identification and management</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC4: Monitoring</strong></td>
                    <td>Ongoing evaluation of controls</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC5: Control Activities</strong></td>
                    <td>Policies and procedures</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC6: Logical & Physical Access</strong></td>
                    <td>Access control, authentication</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC7: System Operations</strong></td>
                    <td>Detecting and responding to incidents</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC8: Change Management</strong></td>
                    <td>Managing system changes</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>CC9: Risk Mitigation</strong></td>
                    <td>Business partner and vendor management</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h2 id="availability"><i class="fas fa-server"></i> 5. Availability Criteria</h2>
        <h3>Key Requirements</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Define and document SLAs (e.g., 99.9% uptime)</li>
            <li>Implement infrastructure redundancy</li>
            <li>Backup and disaster recovery procedures</li>
            <li>Capacity planning and monitoring</li>
            <li>Incident management for outages</li>
            <li>Business continuity planning</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="confidentiality"><i class="fas fa-file-shield"></i> 6. Confidentiality Criteria</h2>
        <h3>Key Requirements</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Data classification scheme</li>
            <li>Encryption at rest and in transit</li>
            <li>Access controls based on need-to-know</li>
            <li>Secure data disposal procedures</li>
            <li>NDAs with employees and contractors</li>
            <li>DLP (Data Loss Prevention) controls</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="privacy"><i class="fas fa-user-lock"></i> 7. Privacy Criteria</h2>
        <h3>Key Requirements</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Privacy notice and consent mechanisms</li>
            <li>Data subject access request procedures</li>
            <li>Data retention and deletion policies</li>
            <li>Privacy impact assessments</li>
            <li>Third-party data sharing agreements</li>
            <li>Breach notification procedures</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="preparation"><i class="fas fa-tasks"></i> 8. Audit Preparation</h2>

        <h3>Timeline for First SOC 2</h3>
        <table>
            <thead>
                <tr>
                    <th>Phase</th>
                    <th>Duration</th>
                    <th>Activities</th>
                </tr>
            </thead>
            <tbody>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Readiness Assessment</strong></td>
                    <td>2-4 weeks</td>
                    <td>Gap analysis, scope definition</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Remediation</strong></td>
                    <td>2-6 months</td>
                    <td>Implement missing controls, document policies</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Control Operation (Type II)</strong></td>
                    <td>6-12 months</td>
                    <td>Run controls, collect evidence</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Audit</strong></td>
                    <td>4-8 weeks</td>
                    <td>Auditor evidence review, testing</td>
                </tr>
                <tr>
                    <td><strong>Report Issuance</strong></td>
                    <td>2-4 weeks</td>
                    <td>Draft review, final report</td>
                </tr>
            </tbody>
        </table>

        <h3>Choosing an Auditor</h3>
        <ul>
            <li>Must be a licensed CPA firm</li>
            <li>Look for experience with your industry/size</li>
            <li>Ask about their testing methodology</li>
            <li>Compare pricing (Type II: $30K-$100K)</li>
            <li>Consider firms like: Drata, Vanta (with partner auditors), or traditional Big 4</li>
        </ul>

        <h2 id="checklist"><i class="fas fa-list-check"></i> 9. Complete Compliance Checklist</h2>

        <h3>Governance & Policies</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Information Security Policy</li>
            <li>Acceptable Use Policy</li>
            <li>Access Control Policy</li>
            <li>Change Management Policy</li>
            <li>Incident Response Plan</li>
            <li>Business Continuity/DR Plan</li>
            <li>Vendor Management Policy</li>
            <li>Data Classification Policy</li>
            <li>Code of Conduct/Ethics Policy</li>
            <li>Risk Assessment Process documented</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Technical Controls</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all access</li>
            <li>Role-based access control (RBAC)</li>
            <li>Encryption at rest (AES-256)</li>
            <li>Encryption in transit (TLS 1.2+)</li>
            <li>Firewall and network segmentation</li>
            <li>Intrusion detection/prevention (IDS/IPS)</li>
            <li>Endpoint protection (EDR/antivirus)</li>
            <li>Vulnerability scanning (at least quarterly)</li>
            <li>Penetration testing (at least annually)</li>
            <li>Centralized logging and monitoring (SIEM)</li>
            <li>Backup and recovery tested regularly</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Operational Controls</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Background checks for employees</li>
            <li>Security awareness training (annual minimum)</li>
            <li>On/offboarding procedures</li>
            <li>Access reviews (quarterly recommended)</li>
            <li>Change management with approvals</li>
            <li>Incident response tested/tabletop exercises</li>
            <li>Vendor security assessments</li>
            <li>Asset inventory maintained</li>
        </ul>

        <h3>Evidence Collection</h3>
        <ul class="checklist">
            <li>Policy acknowledgment records</li>
            <li>Training completion records</li>
            <li>Access review evidence</li>
            <li>Change tickets and approvals</li>
            <li>Vulnerability scan reports</li>
            <li>Penetration test reports</li>
            <li>Incident logs and post-mortems</li>
            <li>Backup restoration test records</li>
        </ul>

        <div class="success-box">
            <strong><i class="fas fa-check-circle"></i> Pro Tips:</strong>
            <ul style="margin-top: 0.5rem; margin-bottom: 0;">
                <li>Use compliance automation tools (Vanta, Drata, Secureframe) to reduce manual work</li>
                <li>Start collecting evidence from day one of your observation period</li>
                <li>Conduct a readiness assessment before engaging an auditor</li>
                <li>Consider SOC 2 + ISO 27001 combined for international customers</li>
            </ul>
        </div>
